title: How America Was Swept by an Anti-Trump Wave
gist: FP Live transcript: Susan Glasser calls the 2026 midterms one of the most decisive rejections of a U.S. president (≈13-pt popular vote margin, 35+ House and up to 8 Senate seat gains), argues corruption rather than just the Iran war drove it, expects Democrats to use appropriations riders to block Trump-Russia deals and pro-Ukraine shifts, sees Gulf allies souring and a Middle East realignment, and says Musk's $500M produced zero wins while AI could define 2028—though she doubts meaningful AI regulation.

insights.claim: Democrats are trending toward a 13-percentage-point popular-vote advantage in the 2026 midterms, the widest Democratic midterm margin since 1976.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: A wave of this size reshapes legislative risk for tariffs, defense and tech policy through 2028.
insights.quote: If you look at the popular vote, it is the widest midterm margin for Democrats since 1976.
insights.locator: Susan Glasser: You have to go

insights.claim: Democrats gained more than 35 House seats and as many as eight Senate seats, a combined swing not seen since the 1946 and 1948 elections.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Supermajority-like Democratic Senate (55 seats) materially raises congressional checks on the executive.
insights.quote: The last time this happened was in 1946 and 1948.
insights.locator: Susan Glasser: You have to go

insights.claim: Glasser says the 2026 result differs from the 1994 wave because the campaign centered on the person of the president, his policies and leadership, making it a resounding referendum on Trump.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Signals Trump's political capital for the final two years is sharply diminished.
insights.locator: What’s different about this election

insights.claim: States like Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas came into play for Democrats in the 2026 blue wave.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: New centrist Democrats from red states may shape a more moderate, populist agenda.
insights.locator: RA: Not in my lifetime

themes.theme: Narrative battle over why Trump lost

insights.claim: Vice President J.D. Vance posted the morning after the election that 'The reason we lost is the [Iran] war,' an almost unprecedented public attack by a vice president on the president's signature policy.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Opens an intra-GOP split that could accelerate pressure to exit the Iran war, easing oil/gas risk premia.
insights.quote: “The reason we lost is the [Iran] war.”
insights.locator: Many of us were quite stunned

insights.claim: Glasser argues Vance and pundits like Sean Hannity blame the Iran war because it absolves them of Trump's other failings and positions Vance for a 2028 presidential run.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Watch GOP repositioning ahead of 2028 that distances from Trump policies.
insights.locator: SG: Vance, according to himself

insights.claim: The Iran war and the resulting price spike were politically disastrous for Trump and Republicans, but Glasser sees the election as a broader repudiation of the Trump administration.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Energy-price shocks are a demonstrated political vulnerability—raising incentive to de-escalate.
insights.quote: In my view, the Iran war and the subsequent spike in prices was quite disastrous for Trump and the Republicans politically.
insights.locator: In my view, the Iran war

insights.claim: A Wall Street Journal survey and others found corruption, not affordability, was the top issue many Americans brought to the polls.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Anti-corruption politics may target Trump-linked business deals and crypto/real-estate ventures.
insights.quote: the top issue many Americans said they were bringing to the polls with them wasn’t affordability but corruption
insights.locator: If you look at a recent Wall Street Journal

insights.claim: Glasser says Trump made more than $2 billion off the presidency in his first year back in office and ranks perceived self-enrichment as her number-one explanation for the outcome.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Expect Democratic oversight investigations into Trump family business dealings.
insights.quote: the president of the United States making more than $2 billion off of the presidency in his first year back in office
insights.locator: If you look at a recent Wall Street Journal

insights.claim: Corruption has been a powerful electoral force in 2026 beyond the U.S., including the Hungarian election that ousted Viktor Orban.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Anti-incumbent, anti-corruption voting trend is a cross-country political risk factor.
insights.locator: Corruption has been a powerful force

insights.claim: Democrats' first tool on national security will be the power of the purse—policy riders on the must-pass defense authorization bill and spending restrictions in appropriations bills.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Defense contractors and war funding become subject to congressional riders; watch NDAA/appropriations language.
insights.quote: The first stop for Democrats looking to affect national security and foreign policy is appropriations bills and the power of the purse.
insights.locator: The first stop for Democrats

insights.claim: Glasser expects at minimum much more aggressive congressional efforts, with bipartisan consensus, to stop Trump from switching sides in the Ukraine war.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Lowers odds of a Russia-favorable settlement and sanctions relief.
insights.locator: The first stop for Democrats

insights.claim: Questionable business deals being discussed between Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and Russian entities—which no American companies want—could be a quick casualty of the midterm result.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: US-Russia commercial/energy deals are at risk of being blocked; reduces sanctions-arbitrage plays.
insights.locator: I think we will see, at a minimum

insights.claim: Chris Coons, the incoming Senate Foreign Relations chairman, did not expect Democrats to reach 55 Senate seats, and the scale of victory may push Democrats to recalibrate their ambitions.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: A 55-seat majority changes what can pass or be blocked.
insights.locator: SG: They may be recalibrating

insights.claim: Trump has posted on Truth Social an image of a red cap reading 'VETO', signaling limits on what the Democratic Congress can enact.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Expect gridlock on legislation; leverage mainly via must-pass bills and oversight.
insights.locator: RA: Let’s talk about what next.

insights.claim: Ravi Agrawal notes Ukraine needs America less today than two years ago as it builds resilience, while the Kremlin is likely worried by the results.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Ukrainian self-reliance (defense industry) reduces dependence on US policy swings.
insights.quote: it’s also clear that Ukraine needs America less today than it did two years ago
insights.locator: RA: I’m imagining that the Kremlin

insights.claim: There is a backlash in both U.S. parties against Trump's unequivocal embrace of Netanyahu and Israel, dramatically so among Democrats.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Shifting US political support for Israel could alter aid and arms-sale dynamics.
insights.locator: SG: There is a backlash in both parties

insights.claim: Glasser says Gulf Arabs have been the engines of much of Trump's foreign policy and 'piggy banks' for him and his family, with vast sums flowing from Gulf interests.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Gulf-Trump financial ties may face Democratic oversight scrutiny.
insights.locator: It’s the Gulf Arabs who have been

insights.claim: A senior Middle East official questioned why Gulf states host U.S. bases and buy U.S. military technology if that is now the reason they are at war, calling it protection money.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Gulf reconsideration of US security ties threatens US arms-export pipeline and petrodollar alignment.
insights.quote: What’s the point of paying the protection money?
insights.locator: But I think the Gulf Arabs

insights.claim: Glasser predicts a rearrangement of Middle East geopolitics and alliances over the next two years, beyond merely escaping the Iran quagmire.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Watch Gulf hedging toward China and other partners; implications for oil policy and defense deals.
insights.quote: We’re likely looking at a rearrangement of a lot of things in the Middle East in the next two years.
insights.locator: But I think the Gulf Arabs

insights.claim: Glasser says Democrats do not yet have a coherent foreign policy; Biden was backward-looking and shaped by Cold War lenses, and a generational shift is underway.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Democratic foreign policy for 2028 is unformed; expect younger candidates and new priorities.
insights.locator: Democrats do not have one single coherent view.

insights.claim: Nearly 20 new senators are arriving with an average age in the 50s, an unusually high Senate turnover that people have underappreciated.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Generational turnover may reshape Senate stances on China, tech and alliances.
insights.quote: A huge percentage of the Senate is turning over, a much higher percentage than is normal.
insights.locator: Democrats do not have one single coherent view.

themes.theme: Big Tech, Musk and AI politics

insights.claim: Elon Musk spent about $500 million on the 2026 elections—more than any individual in history by a large margin—and won literally zero victories.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Demonstrates limits of tech-billionaire political spending; raises political risk for Musk-linked firms.
insights.quote: That obscene amount of money produced literally zero victories for him.
insights.locator: SG: It is incredible.

insights.claim: Voters rejected data centers and supported candidates promising regulation, fitting a Democratic center/center-left populism against billionaire-crony capitalism.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Local opposition to data centers is a real headwind for AI infrastructure buildout (siting, power, permitting).
insights.quote: They’ve rejected data centers. They’ve supported candidates who promised regulation.
insights.locator: One thing that we haven’t touched on

insights.claim: Glasser is pessimistic that the new Democratic Congress will pass major AI regulation, noting Congress punted on regulating the internet era.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: Near-term federal AI regulatory risk remains low despite the anti-tech mood.
insights.quote: So I’m very pessimistic about major legislation.
insights.locator: Does it mean the new Democratic Congress

insights.claim: Glasser predicts AI could be the defining issue of the 2028 presidential election, displacing Trump as the focus.
insights.speaker: Susan Glasser
insights.so_what: AI policy becomes a 2028 political flashpoint—watch for campaign pledges on data centers, jobs and regulation.
insights.quote: We may be talking a lot less about Trump and a lot more about AI.
insights.locator: Does it mean the new Democratic Congress
